rationale: Start with a broad scouting gradient at moderate temperature to elute all 10 compounds if possible and map the overall retention window without excessive compression. This should reveal whether peaks are unretained, bunched in the gradient, or still eluting in the hold so later runs can tighten the window and adjust slope.

All 10 compounds eluted early and fully resolved, so the main opportunity is to cut the time penalty by trimming the gradient window to the actual elution region. Based on the observed retention times, a narrower window around the estimated elution compositions should keep all peaks in-gradient while shortening the last peak substantially.

The broad window was clearly better; narrowing phi1 slowed the late peak too much, so the next lever is a steeper gradient to reduce the time term while checking whether the critical mid-run pair loses much resolution. Comparing this directly to injection 1 isolates slope sensitivity because only tG changes.

The critical cluster around peaks 5–7 is strongly slope-sensitive: halving tG gave a great time gain but collapsed that region. An intermediate gradient should recover enough resolution in the 5–7 cluster while likely keeping the run short enough to preserve or improve the current CRF.

The best point so far is near the slope where the 6/7 pair is just becoming acceptable; a small increase in tG from 14 to 16 min should test whether that pair crosses into fully acceptable resolution while likely keeping the time penalty at zero. This is a focused refinement around the current optimum.

Since tG 14 min is very close to optimal, the remaining gain may come from modest temperature-induced selectivity changes for the stubborn 6/7 pair without incurring a time penalty. Lowering T slightly is a targeted test to see whether that near-critical pair separates better than at 40 C while staying within the zero-penalty time region.

Lowering temperature hurt selectivity by shifting the critical overlap from 6/7 to 5/6, so test the opposite direction at the otherwise optimal 14 min slope. A modest increase to 45 C may improve the 5–7 cluster selectivity while likely preserving the short run time.

Temperature moves were detrimental, so return to 40 C and refine only the slope around the apparent optimum. Testing 12 min checks whether a slightly faster run than 14 min can still keep the critical 5–7 cluster resolved well enough to beat the current best CRF.

Since all peaks elute by 9.4 min at 14 min tG, slightly lowering phi1 may shift selectivity in the dense 5–7 cluster without pushing the last peak too late. This tests whether a modestly narrower high-end window can improve the limiting pair while staying near the current optimum conditions.

The move from phi1 0.95 to 0.90 improved the limiting 6/7 pair while keeping the run in the zero time-penalty region, so continue in the same direction with a small additional decrease in phi1. This should show whether selectivity for that cluster keeps improving before the last peak is pushed too late.

The best condition so far is phi1 0.90 at 14 min, and the 6/7 pair still limits the score slightly; making the gradient a bit shallower should improve that pair further. This tests whether the gain in resolution outweighs any small time penalty, analogous to how 16 min improved resolution at phi1 0.95.

The best region is clearly around phi1 0.90 and tG 14, so now probe the low-end boundary: slightly increasing phi0 may alter selectivity in the crowded mid-gradient cluster while keeping all peaks retained and within the zero-penalty time window. Raising phi0 to 0.10 improved the best method, and lowering phi1 from 0.90 to 0.85 previously improved the critical pair at the cost of only a slight time increase. A perfect method is already in hand, so use remaining budget to probe robustness on the low-organic side of the window. Increasing phi0 one step while keeping the successful phi1 and tG tests whether the optimum is broad or sharply tuned around the current start composition.

Another perfect score at higher phi0 suggests a broad optimum, so continue mapping that plateau by increasing phi0 one more step. This checks how far the start composition can be raised before early peaks become too compressed or effectively unretained.

This confirms whether tG 14 is truly the sweet spot or whether the same window remains optimal over a broader slope range.

With the global maximum already reached, the remaining value is in checking whether a temperature change can preserve perfect performance at one of the best windows. Since higher temperature badly degraded the critical 6/7 separation, use one remaining run to test the opposite direction at the other perfect-score window. This checks whether the optimal window remains robust to a lower temperature or if 40 C is uniquely required for maximum performance.
